address_cn: 上海市黄浦区中山东一路北至外白渡桥、南至十六铺码头
hook: A 1.5-kilometer waterfront where 52 colonial-era buildings face off against the futuristic Pudong skyline across the Huangpu River — the single most iconic view in China's most cosmopolitan city, and it's completely free.
honest_description: The Bund is Shanghai's definitive postcard view and it genuinely delivers. The contrast between the stately 1920s European banks on one side and the glittering Pudong towers on the other is visually stunning and deeply symbolic of Shanghai's past-meets-future identity. The experience transforms with the time of day: mornings are peaceful with locals doing tai chi, afternoons let you appreciate the architectural details, and nighttime — when the entire skyline erupts in light — is legitimately world-class. That said, it's essentially a long riverside walk with a great view; there's no museum to enter or activity to do beyond strolling, photographing, and perhaps taking a river cruise. Weekend and holiday evenings are sardine-level crowded with police managing one-way pedestrian flow. The dining options directly on the Bund are overpriced tourist traps — the good food is a few blocks away. Best for anyone visiting Shanghai for the first time; skip it if you've already seen it or hate crowds.

foreigner_top_questions.question: When exactly do the lights turn on and off?
foreigner_top_questions.answer: The building illuminations turn on around 6:00 PM in winter and 7:00 PM in summer, and switch off at 10:00-11:00 PM (most commonly 10:00 PM on weekdays, 11:00 PM on weekends/holidays). The light show on the Pudong skyscrapers typically starts around 7:30-8:30 PM. Plan to arrive 30-60 minutes before lights-on to secure a good spot and watch the transition from sunset to illumination — this is universally the most recommended timing.

foreigner_top_questions.question: Is the river cruise worth it, and how much does it cost?
foreigner_top_questions.answer: The Huangpu River cruise (approximately ¥120-150 for a 45-60 minute sightseeing cruise from Shiliupu Pier) gives you a unique water-level perspective of both banks and is widely recommended by visitors. However, the budget alternative is the regular commuter ferry for just ¥2 — it crosses the river in 10 minutes and gives you essentially the same views for a fraction of the price. The ferry dock is at Jinling East Road. The sightseeing cruise is better after dark; the ferry works anytime.

experience_format_note: Open-air waterfront promenade — completely free, no tickets needed, open 24/7. Simply walk along the elevated riverside platform at your own pace. The promenade runs 1.5 km from the Waibaidu Bridge (north) to the Shiliupu Pier (south). There's no set route or required direction. The Bund Sightseeing Tunnel (¥50 one-way, ¥70 return) runs under the river to Pudong but is widely considered underwhelming for the price — the ¥2 ferry is better value.
vibe: Cinematic, bustling, and romantic — like standing on the boundary between two centuries, surrounded by thousands of people having the same 'wow' moment.

time_needed.quick_visit: 30-60 minutes (walk one direction along the promenade, snap photos, leave)
time_needed.recommended: 2-3 hours (arrive before sunset, watch the lights come on, walk the full length, take the ferry across)
time_needed.deep_dive: Half day (combine with Nanjing Road walk, river cruise, explore the historic buildings, cross to Pudong side)

best_time.best_time_of_day: Arrive 30-60 minutes before sunset to catch golden hour light on the colonial buildings, then stay through the lighting ceremony. The transition from dusk to full illumination is the highlight. Early morning (6:00 AM) offers a completely different, peaceful experience with locals exercising.
best_time.worst_time: Chinese public holidays (especially National Day October 1-7, May Day, Chinese New Year) and weekend evenings from 7-9 PM — the crowds become genuinely overwhelming with police implementing one-way pedestrian flow control.
best_time.seasonal_notes: Spring (March-May) and autumn (September-November) offer the most comfortable weather. Summer is hot and humid with limited shade on the promenade. Winter is cold with biting river wind — dress warmly. Clear days give the best skyline views; fog and smog can obscure the Pudong towers.
best_time.pro_tip: Visit on a weekday evening for the lights with manageable crowds. For photos without people, come at 6:00 AM. After 10:00 PM the lights dim and crowds thin — still beautiful but less dramatic. The north end near Waibaidu Bridge and the south end near Shiliupu Pier are always less crowded than the central section opposite the Oriental Pearl Tower.

getting_in.opening_hours: Open 24/7 year-round. Free admission. Building illuminations: approximately 6:00-10:00 PM (winter) / 7:00-11:00 PM (summer), extended during holidays.

price_breakdown.highlight: 45-60 minute cruise from Shiliupu Pier, best at night
10-minute ride to Pudong — budget alternative to the cruise with great views
646m underground ride to Pudong — underwhelming light show, not recommended by most visitors

getting_in.booking_required: No — completely open access. River cruise tickets can be purchased on-site at Shiliupu Pier or via Trip.com.
getting_in.booking_method: No booking needed for the Bund itself. River cruises can be booked at the pier ticket counters or online via Trip.com/Klook. Our team can also book river cruise tickets for you and arrange the timing to fit your evening plan.
getting_in.passport_accepted: Not applicable — no tickets or ID required for the Bund. River cruise tickets can be purchased without ID.
getting_in.what_to_bring: Camera/phone with charged battery. Light jacket for evening river wind (even in summer). Comfortable walking shoes. Water bottle (limited vendors along the promenade). Power bank.
getting_in.queue_situation: No queue for the Bund itself. On busy evenings, police may implement one-way pedestrian flow control at access stairways, causing 5-15 minute waits to get onto the promenade. The central section opposite the Oriental Pearl Tower is the most congested area.
getting_in.language_barrier_rating: easy-no-chinese-needed — It's a public walkway with no tickets, guides, or staff interaction needed. Signage is bilingual. River cruise announcements are in Chinese and English.

highlights.name: The Pudong Skyline Night View
highlights.description: The iconic view across the Huangpu River to the Oriental Pearl Tower, Shanghai Tower (3rd tallest building in the world), Jin Mao Tower, and Shanghai World Financial Center. When illuminated at night, the synchronized light displays on these skyscrapers create one of the world's most spectacular urban vistas.
highlights.foreigner_note: This is THE Shanghai photo. The Oriental Pearl Tower is the bulbous retro-futuristic one, the Shanghai Tower is the twisting tallest one, and the 'bottle opener' is the World Financial Center.
highlights.tip: The best unobstructed view is from the central promenade section near Chen Yi Square. For less crowded photos, walk to the northern end near Waibaidu Bridge or the southern end near Shiliupu Pier.

highlights.name: The Colonial Architecture (万国建筑博览群)
highlights.description: 52 buildings in Gothic, Baroque, Neoclassical, and Art Deco styles line the western side of the Bund — a living museum of early 20th-century architecture built during Shanghai's era as an international trading port. Notable buildings include the Peace Hotel, the former HSBC Building (now Shanghai Pudong Development Bank), and the Customs House with its clock tower.
highlights.foreigner_note: These buildings represent the colonial era when foreign powers controlled Shanghai's trade — British, French, American, and Japanese banks and trading houses. The HSBC Building has a stunning mosaic ceiling you can peek at during banking hours.
highlights.tip: The buildings are best appreciated during daytime when you can see the architectural details. In the evening, the warm golden illumination is beautiful but obscures the fine details. Walk on the street side (west) rather than the river side to get closer to the facades.

highlights.name: Waibaidu Bridge (外白渡桥)
highlights.description: A historic steel truss bridge at the northern end of the Bund, spanning Suzhou Creek where it meets the Huangpu River. Built in 1907, it's one of Shanghai's most recognizable landmarks and offers excellent photo angles of both the colonial buildings and the Pudong skyline.
highlights.foreigner_note: Featured in numerous Chinese films and TV dramas set in 1930s Shanghai. The bridge marks the former boundary between the British and American concessions.
highlights.tip: Stand on the bridge at sunset facing south for a stunning composition with the Bund buildings and Pudong skyline together. Much less crowded than the main promenade.

highlights.name: Huangpu River Cruise / Ferry
highlights.description: Sightseeing cruises depart from Shiliupu Pier for 45-60 minute journeys up and down the river, offering a water-level perspective of both banks. The budget alternative is the ¥2 commuter ferry from Jinling East Road pier, which crosses to Pudong in 10 minutes.
highlights.foreigner_note: The ¥2 ferry is one of the best-value experiences in Shanghai — locals use it for commuting, but for tourists it's a scenic mini-cruise. No booking needed, just tap a transit card or pay cash.
highlights.tip: Take the ferry at dusk for the best light. For the sightseeing cruise, the top deck offers the best views but can be cold and windy — bring a jacket even in summer.

what_visitors_miss.what: North Bund (北外滩) across Suzhou Creek
what_visitors_miss.why: Same stunning Pudong skyline view but with a fraction of the crowds. Recently developed with modern landscaping, it's where savvy locals go for photos. Cross Waibaidu Bridge and walk north along the riverfront.

what_visitors_miss.what: Waitanyuan (外滩源) — The Origin of the Bund
what_visitors_miss.why: A beautifully restored European-style compound at the northern end of the Bund with cafes, galleries, and architecture. Perfect for photos with the Lujiazui skyline backdrop but far fewer tourists than the main promenade.

A completely different experience — locals practice tai chi, run along the promenade, play saxophones in the park, and stretch. The Bund feels like it belongs to the city rather than to tourists. Peaceful, authentic, and photogenic with soft morning light.

strategy.smart_route: Take Metro Line 2 or 10 to East Nanjing Road station → walk east along Nanjing Road Pedestrian Street toward the river (10-15 minutes) → arrive at the central Bund near Chen Yi Square → walk north along the promenade to Waibaidu Bridge → cross the bridge to Waitanyuan for less crowded photos → return south along the promenade to Shiliupu Pier → take the ¥2 ferry to Pudong → view the colonial buildings from the Pudong waterfront → return by ferry or metro.
strategy.what_to_skip: The Bund Sightseeing Tunnel (¥50-70) is universally considered overpriced for a tacky light show in a small cart — take the ¥2 ferry instead. The street photographers who aggressively offer to take your photo will charge ¥30+ per image and pressure you to buy all of them. The rooftop bars directly on the Bund charge premium prices (¥100+ for a cocktail) — if you want a drink with a view, the Waldorf Astoria terrace offers free access without mandatory purchase.
strategy.pro_tips: Download DiDi (Chinese Uber) before visiting — getting a taxi from the Bund at night is extremely difficult due to traffic and one-way streets. The metro is the most reliable way to leave. For the best photos of the Pudong skyline, use portrait mode from the central promenade railing during blue hour (20-30 minutes after sunset). Bring a portable charger — you'll take hundreds of photos. If you want a proper dinner with a view that is not a tourist trap, message our concierge team — we can recommend and reserve a table at a restaurant that locals actually rate highly.

heads_up.warning: Extremely crowded on weekend and holiday evenings
heads_up.advice: Police implement one-way pedestrian flow during peak times. You may not be able to stop walking or find railing space for photos in the central section. Visit on a weekday evening or walk to the less crowded north/south ends.

The 'tea ceremony scam' is infamous: friendly English-speaking young people approach you, chat warmly, then invite you to a 'traditional tea ceremony' where you're charged ¥200-2000. Politely decline any stranger who initiates conversation and invites you somewhere. Also beware of aggressive street photographers who snap many photos then demand payment for all. If someone has already lured you into a suspicious situation, message our team immediately — we can call the venue on your behalf, help you leave, or contact police if needed.

heads_up.warning: Limited food and restroom options on the promenade itself
heads_up.advice: The restaurants directly facing the Bund are overpriced tourist traps. Walk 2-3 blocks inland to Zhapu Road or side streets off Nanjing Road for authentic, affordable Shanghai food. Public restrooms exist along the promenade but are crowded and not always well-maintained.

heads_up.warning: Getting a taxi/DiDi after 9 PM is very difficult
heads_up.advice: Traffic around the Bund at night is gridlocked. Plan to leave by metro (last trains around 10:30 PM) or walk a few blocks away from the Bund to hail a ride from a quieter street. If you are stuck and cannot get a ride, message our concierge — we can arrange a pickup from a quieter street nearby.

foreigners_watch_out: The 'tea scam' is the number one tourist trap in Shanghai: English-speaking university-age locals approach you for friendly conversation, then invite you to an expensive tea shop or bar. You'll be pressured to pay ¥500-2000. Never follow a stranger to a shop, no matter how friendly they seem.

Street photographers will offer to take your photo, snap 15-20 images rapidly, then demand ¥30+ per photo. If you don't want photos, firmly say no before they start shooting. If they do take unwanted photos, you are not obligated to pay.
Google Maps does not work in China without a VPN. Download Amap (高德地图) or Apple Maps (works in China) before arriving. DiDi is the ride-hailing app (Chinese Uber).

The Bund area has strong police presence and is very safe, even late at night. Violent crime is essentially nonexistent here, but pickpocketing in dense crowds is possible — keep valuables in front pockets.
Lights turn off at 10:00-11:00 PM sharp — many tourists arrive too late and miss the illumination. Plan to be on the promenade by 7:00 PM at the latest.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: The skyline is obscured by fog or smog
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: Check the weather/air quality before heading out. If visibility is poor, the experience is significantly diminished. Fog tends to clear by midday — try visiting in the afternoon instead of evening.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: Walk along the Bund anyway to appreciate the colonial architecture up close, or head to the Shanghai Tower observation deck (632m) where you'll be above the fog layer on most days.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: The crowds are unbearable and you can't find space
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: Walk to the far north end (past Waibaidu Bridge toward North Bund) or the far south end (Shiliupu Pier area) — same views, dramatically fewer people.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: Cross to the Pudong side via the ¥2 ferry and enjoy the reverse view of the colonial buildings from the Binjiang Avenue waterfront — it's equally beautiful and much less crowded.

if_things_go_wrong.problem: Phone died and you can't navigate back
if_things_go_wrong.what_to_do: Walk west (away from the river) to reach Zhongshan East Road, then continue west to reach Nanjing Road or any major street. Follow signs for 南京东路站 (Nanjing East Road Station) — Metro Lines 2 and 10.
if_things_go_wrong.plan_b: Any taxi driver or local will understand '南京东路地铁站' (Nánjīng Dōng Lù dìtiě zhàn). The Bund is one of the most well-known locations in Shanghai. If you reach any phone or borrowed device, message our team through WhatsApp and we can guide you or arrange a pickup.

preparation.what_to_wear: Comfortable walking shoes — you'll walk 5,000-10,000+ steps on flat pavement. Bring a light jacket even in summer for the evening river breeze. In winter (December-February), the wind chill off the Huangpu River is brutal — dress in warm layers with a windproof outer layer.
preparation.what_to_bring: Fully charged phone with power bank. Camera if you want quality night photos (phone cameras struggle with low light at distance). Water bottle. Small bag for personal items — keep it in front in crowds.
preparation.what_not_to_bring: Drones (strictly prohibited — repeated loudspeaker announcements warn against them). Tripods may attract unwanted attention from security during peak hours. Large luggage.

physical_accessibility.physical_details: Completely flat paved promenade with ramp access. The 1.5 km walk is gentle and suitable for all fitness levels. Wheelchair accessible throughout the main promenade. Benches are available but often occupied during busy times.
physical_accessibility.age_notes: Suitable for all ages including young children and elderly. Stroller-friendly. No stairs required on the main promenade (some access points have both stairs and ramps).
physical_accessibility.health_warnings: Summer heat and humidity can be intense with no shade on the promenade — bring water and sun protection. Winter wind chill is significant. The dense evening crowds may cause anxiety for those uncomfortable in tight spaces.

concierge_opportunities.platform: Trip.com, Klook, or purchase at Shiliupu Pier ticket counter
concierge_opportunities.value_to_user: A unique water-level perspective of both the colonial buildings and Pudong skyline. Evening cruises (¥120-150) are the most popular option. Book in advance during holidays to guarantee a spot.

concierge_opportunities.action: Book a rooftop bar/restaurant with Bund view
concierge_opportunities.platform: OpenTable, Trip.com, or direct restaurant booking
concierge_opportunities.value_to_user: Elevated views without the street-level crowds. POP at Bund 3 (¥50 coffee minimum), Vue Bar at Hyatt on the Bund, and Flair at The Ritz-Carlton Pudong all offer spectacular views. Reserve window/terrace seats in advance.

useful_chinese.english: I want to go to the Bund

pair_with.suggestion: Nanjing Road Pedestrian Street (南京路步行街)
pair_with.why: Shanghai's most famous shopping street leads directly to the Bund — walk it on the way there or back. Mix of international brands, local shops, and street food. The pedestrian street is beautifully lit at night.
pair_with.travel_time: 10-15 minute walk from the Bund (connected directly)

pair_with.why: A classical Chinese garden and bazaar area just 10 minutes south of the Bund. Perfect morning activity before an evening Bund visit — see traditional Shanghai before modern Shanghai.
pair_with.travel_time: 10-15 minute walk south along the river, or 1 metro stop

pair_with.suggestion: Pudong Lujiazui (Shanghai Tower, Oriental Pearl Tower)
pair_with.why: Cross the river to see the skyline up close. The Shanghai Tower observation deck (¥180) at 546 meters offers panoramic views including back toward the Bund. Take the ¥2 ferry for the crossing itself.
pair_with.travel_time: 10 minutes by ferry, 5 minutes by metro (Line 2)

cultural_context: The Bund tells the story of modern China in a single panoramic view. The colonial buildings on the west bank were built by foreign powers who controlled Shanghai's trade from the 1840s through the 1940s — a period Chinese history calls the 'Century of Humiliation.' Across the river, the Pudong skyline — which was farmland as recently as 1990 — represents China's extraordinary economic transformation. For Chinese visitors, the Bund is not just scenic; it's a powerful visual metaphor for national resurgence. Understanding this context adds emotional depth to what might otherwise feel like just a pretty skyline.

photo_spots.location: Central promenade railing opposite Oriental Pearl Tower
photo_spots.tip: Arrive 30 minutes before sunset for blue hour. Use portrait mode for the skyline. The railing is the most fought-over photo spot — weekday evenings or early morning for fewer people.
photo_spots.why: The classic Shanghai postcard shot with the Pearl Tower, Shanghai Tower, and Jin Mao Tower all in frame. The water reflections at night add magic.

photo_spots.tip: Sunset is ideal. Stand on the west side of the bridge for the Bund buildings and Pudong skyline in one frame.
photo_spots.why: Includes the historic bridge structure as foreground with the full Bund panorama behind — a more unique composition than the standard railing shot.

photo_spots.tip: Take the ¥2 ferry across and walk along the Pudong waterfront. The colonial buildings photographed from this side are equally stunning, especially when illuminated.
photo_spots.why: The reverse view that most tourists miss — the golden-lit colonial architecture reflected in the river, with far fewer people competing for space.

photo_spots.location: Waitanyuan (外滩源) at the north end
photo_spots.tip: The European-style buildings here frame the Lujiazui skyline beautifully. Much less crowded for creative compositions.
photo_spots.why: Combines restored historical architecture in the foreground with the modern skyline — a more sophisticated, less touristy shot.

card_hook: Where old Shanghai stares down new Shanghai across a river.
